summary: Construction, remodeling and repair of real property are not subject to South Dakota sales tax; the prime contractor instead owes a 2% contractor's excise tax on its gross receipts.

conditions.when: Floor-covering installation (SIC 1752: carpet, vinyl, laminate, hardwood, linoleum, resilient flooring); ceramic tile, marble, terrazzo and similar remain under contractor's excise tax

citations.title: SD DOR, Sales and Use Tax Guide (July 2026)
citations.quote: Construction services taxed in chapter 10-46A or 10-46B are not subject to sales tax.

citations.title: SDCL 10-45-12.1
citations.quote: construction services (division C) except industry no. 1752 and locksmiths and locksmith shops

citations.title: SD DOR, Contractor's Excise Tax Guide (July 2026)
citations.quote: This includes repair or remodeling of existing real property or the construction of a new project.

citations.title: SDCL 10-46A-1
citations.quote: There is imposed an excise tax upon the gross receipts of all prime contractors engaged in realty improvement contracts, at the rate of two percent.

citations.title: SD DOR Tax Fact: Flooring (July 2023)
citations.quote: Sales tax applies to the sale of and the installation of the following floor material:

notes: Both subcodes (improvement and repair) are construction services exempt from sales tax under SDCL 10-45-12.1 and subject instead to the 2% contractor's excise tax (SDCL 10-46A), which the prime contractor owes on gross receipts and may list on the invoice; that excise tax is not a sales tax and isn't modeled. Contractors pay sales/use tax on materials. Utility projects fall under SDCL 10-46B (also 2% excise). Locksmiths and floor laying are carved out of the construction exemption and are sales-taxable. Snow removal, landscaping maintenance and similar services are sales-taxable services, not construction. 10-45-12.1's text was last amended by SL 2004 ch 94.

summary: Supplying and installing floor covering (carpet, vinyl, hardwood, laminate) is subject to sales tax, unlike other construction services.

summary: A seller's delivery charge on goods exempt at that sale is not taxable in South Dakota.

citations.title: SD DOR, Sales and Use Tax Guide (July 2026), Delivery Charges
citations.quote: Delivery charges are included in the gross receipts and are subject to the same sales or use tax rate as the product or service. If the product or service is not taxable, the delivery charge is not taxable.

citations.title: SD DOR Tax Fact: Shipping and Transportation (January 2026)
citations.quote: If the product is not taxable, the delivery and handling charges are not taxable.

notes: Few goods are exempt in SD (groceries are taxable); this applies to e.g. sales for resale, sales to exempt entities, or exempt products. For mixed shipments the taxable share is allocated by price or weight (ARSD 64:06:01:10, per the Shipping fact).

summary: A seller's delivery charge on taxable goods is part of gross receipts and taxed at the same state and municipal rate as the goods.

citations.title: SD DOR, Sales and Use Tax Guide (July 2026), Delivery Charges
citations.quote: Delivery charges are included in the gross receipts and are subject to the same sales or use tax rate as the product or service. If the product or service is not taxable, the delivery charge is not taxable.

citations.title: SD DOR Tax Fact: Shipping and Transportation (January 2026)
citations.quote: A retailer’s charge for delivery and handling of taxable products is subject to the South Dakota state sales tax and applicable municipal sales tax when the taxable product is delivered in South Dakota.

notes: Delivery billed by a transportation company the customer hires directly is not the seller's delivery charge. SDCL 10-45-1(4) defines delivery charges (SSUTA definition, adopted before 2018).

summary: Candy is taxed in South Dakota at the full state rate plus municipal sales tax, like all food.

citations.quote: upon the gross receipts of all sales of tangible personal property consisting of goods, wares, or merchandise, except as otherwise provided in this chapter

citations.title: SD DOR, Sales and Use Tax Guide (July 2026), Exemptions
citations.quote: Food Stamp Purchases - All food stamp purchases (SNAP) are not subject to sales tax.

citations.title: SD DOR, Sales and Use Tax Guide (July 2026)
citations.quote: The sales tax applies to the gross receipts of all retail sales, including the sale, lease, or rental of personal property or any product transferred electronically, and the sale of services.

notes: South Dakota has no general food exemption: food is tangible personal property taxed at the full state rate plus municipal sales tax; the only food exemptions are SNAP and WIC purchases (SDCL 10-45-14.7, 10-45-14.8). No DOR page states 'groceries are taxable' in one sentence; the rule rests on SDCL 10-45-2 (all sales of goods unless excepted) and the DOR's list of exemptions, which names only SNAP/WIC. The 2023-07-01 state rate cut (4.5% to 4.2%, scheduled to revert 2027-07-01 per SDCL 10-45-2's future text) is a rate change, not a taxability change, and isn't modeled. Food was taxable before 2018; earlier history not checked. Legislative and ballot attempts to exempt groceries (e.g. IM 28, 2024) were reported by news sources as failed; not verified against an official canvass, and no exemption appears in SDCL 10-45 as of 2026-10.

summary: Catering is subject to South Dakota state sales tax and municipal sales tax where the event is held.

citations.title: SD DOR Tax Fact: Bars and Restaurants (July 2026)
citations.quote: Catering services are subject to state sales tax, the municipal sales, and municipal gross receipts tax rate based on the location of the catered event.

citations.title: SDCL 10-45-4
citations.quote: Any service as defined by § 10-45-4.1 shall be taxable, unless the service is specifically exempt from the provisions of this chapter.

notes: Catering also bears the municipal gross receipts tax (MGRT) where the city imposes it; MGRT is a separate tax not modeled here. The Bars and Restaurants fact is dated July 2026; the services tax (SDCL 10-45-4) predates 2018.
